analysis.one_liner: Bans new mining on about one million acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have removed about 982,550 acres of federal land around the Grand Canyon — the Tusayan Ranger District and land near Kanab Creek and House Rock Valley — from the mining laws that let companies stake claims and extract minerals [S2] [S3]. It would have barred new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing on that land, while leaving any existing valid mining rights untouched [S2] [S3]. The area sits in the watersheds that drain into the Colorado River through the Grand Canyon, where a new uranium mining boom has been a live controversy for years. The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and to two subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: People who rely on water flowing through the Grand Canyon region — including Colorado River water users across the Southwest — would benefit from keeping uranium and other hardrock mining out of the watersheds that feed the river. Outdoor recreation, tourism businesses around the Grand Canyon, and nearby tribal communities concerned about contamination would also benefit. Existing mining claim holders are protected because the bill respects valid, existing rights [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Water users and Grand Canyon-area communities

how_it_helps.text: Withdraws roughly 982,550 acres around the Grand Canyon from staking new mining claims, mineral leasing, geothermal leasing, and mineral materials extraction [S2] [S3].
Keeps mining activity out of the watersheds draining into the Grand Canyon and the Colorado River, the source of drinking and irrigation water for much of the Southwest [S2].
Protects existing rights holders: any valid mining rights in place before enactment are unaffected, and if such rights are later relinquished, the land becomes protected then [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies that could otherwise stake new claims, and mineral lessees who could otherwise drill, on that land. The federal government forgoes potential mineral revenue and royalties from the withdrawn acres. In principle, the public gives up whatever minerals under those acres are worth — the tradeoff the bill makes in exchange for watershed protection.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mining companies with future claims there

drawbacks.text: The withdrawal permanently removes about 982,550 acres from mineral development, forgoing whatever mineral value — including domestic uranium supply — lies under them [S2].
The bill is a broad, one-size-fits-all withdrawal rather than a mine-by-mine review, so land with little contamination risk is protected along with the most sensitive watershed acreage [S2].
Because it grandfathered valid existing rights, contamination from operations already claimed before enactment would not have been prevented [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is water quality against mineral access. The bill's safeguarding of roughly a million acres of Grand Canyon watershed carries real but diffuse benefits — clean water for millions of downstream users and protection of a national icon — while the cost is concentrated on mining companies and forgone federal mineral revenue, a small share of national mineral supply. The grandfather clause means the strongest objection is not lost jobs today but forgone development tomorrow. On balance the protection outweighs the cost, though the blanket withdrawal is less tailored than a site-specific review would be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee, which passed it down to two subcommittees, and neither the full committee nor the House ever took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 21, 2013 by Rep. Raúl Grijalva with 14 Democratic cosponsors [S1] [S4].

Referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and a week later to the Subcommittee on Public Lands and Environmental Regulation and the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the bill died in committee when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies with an interest in staking new claims or drilling on federal land near the Grand Canyon are better off, since the land remains open to entry and leasing. The committee leadership that declined to act avoided a fight over a mineral withdrawal on its watch.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining interests and the inactive committee

for.name: Rep. Raúl Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to withdraw about one million acres of Grand Canyon watershed land from the mining laws.

for.name: 14 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Arizona members Kirkpatrick and Pastor alongside members from New York, Colorado, Minnesota, and other states.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; after referring it to two subcommittees, no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 14 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the Republican-run Natural Resources Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have closed roughly a million acres near the Grand Canyon to new mining claims and leases, eliminating future mine sites. Keeping the land open preserves the industry's ability to stake claims in watersheds that feed the Colorado River, where contamination risk falls on downstream water users, not on the companies.

industries.industry: Grand Canyon tourism and recreation businesses
industries.note: A mining withdrawal protects the landscape and water quality that draw millions of visitors to the Grand Canyon, protecting the tourism economy that depends on it.
The bill would have withdrawn the same acres from mineral and geothermal leasing, ending leasing access on that land.
